# workloadctl

> Declarative rootless workload manager for Linux. Define workloads as TOML files, and workloadctl handles user creation, systemd service generation, volume management, secrets, and lifecycle across two **substrates** — isolated rootless-podman containers and KVM/QEMU virtual machines.

workloadctl is a Python CLI tool and systemd integration that turns TOML config files into fully isolated workloads. A workload is either a **container** (rootless podman, the common case) or a **VM** (raw QEMU/KVM, declared with a `[vm]` section). Each container workload gets a dedicated locked-down system user (`_wl-<name>`), its own UID/subuid namespace, a systemd service generated at boot, automatic volume directories, and optional TPM2-encrypted secrets via systemd credentials; VM workloads get a per-instance disk set, bridge networking, and cloud-init seed. The two substrates share one TOML model and one day-2 verb surface, dispatched through a **Substrate port** (see "Substrate dispatch").

## Requirements

- Fedora 41+ (or any systemd + Podman 5.3+ Linux)
- Python 3.11+
- Works on standard Fedora or bootc/immutable OS images

## Architecture

The system has four main components:

1. **Generator + early-boot oneshot**: A tiny shell systemd generator (`generators/workload-generator`) emits a single oneshot service unit, `workload-generate.service`. That service runs the Python script `generators/workload-generate` during early boot (ordered `After=sysinit.target Before=basic.target`), which reads `/etc/workloads.d/*/workload.toml` and produces systemd-sysusers configs and per-workload service unit files in `/run/systemd/system/`. The Python work is *not* run as a systemd generator because generators are expected to be fast and minimal (see `systemd.generator(7)`); Python import overhead alone can exceed the generator execution budget systemd 258+ enforces. Both the shell generator and the Python script always exit 0 so a failure never blocks boot. The Python script is still read-only with respect to `/var` — all `/var` work is deferred to `workload-ensure-user` at service start.

   **Boot cost, measured (2026-07-28, on a deliberately slow dev host — Fedora 44 / systemd 259).** `workload-generate.service` is ordered `Before=basic.target`, so its whole runtime is boot delay. It is **~0.65s, near-flat in workload count**: 615ms at 1 workload, 715ms at 40. The breakdown, from phase-instrumented boots: ~180ms Python startup + `lib/` imports, ~400ms `systemctl daemon-reload`, ~30ms for the batched start enqueue, and only **~2ms per workload** for everything the generator actually does (TOML parse, validation, unit emission, UID allocation combined — 77ms for all 40). The shell generator that emits the oneshot is O(1) at 3–8ms, well inside the `systemd.generator(7)` budget the split exists to respect. So the cost is two fixed constants, not a scaling problem; if this ever needs to come down further, `daemon-reload` is the target, and micro-optimising the config loop is not worth doing. Do not re-derive this by reading the code — the code path that dominates is invisible in a non-live run (it is gated on `SERVICES_DIR == /run/systemd/system`), which is why the number went unmeasured for so long. Reproduce with a bench-bundle sweep + reboot, reading `systemctl show workload-generate.service -p ExecMainStartTimestampMonotonic -p ExecMainExitTimestampMonotonic`.

   The CLI re-runs `workload-generate` post-boot to apply config edits (`enable`, `edit`, `recreate`), and those runs pass **`--workload <name>`**, which narrows the emit to one workload, plus **`--no-start`**, which suppresses the generator's own daemon-reload + `systemctl start` enqueue. Boot passes neither and emits the whole enabled set. Both flags matter: an unfiltered run rewrites *every* enabled workload's unit files and enqueues a `systemctl start` for each, so acting on one workload would (a) silently update a bystander's unit file in `/run` while its service keeps running the old one — and `drift` compares against the files, so the staleness becomes invisible — and (b) start a workload the operator had deliberately stopped. And a generator-enqueued start fires *during* the CLI verb's generate step, racing ahead of the verb's later provisioning — most critically `enable`'s image transfer to the user store, where the premature cold start pins a fresh container to the stale image (the verbs own their start/restart after those steps instead). The `--workload` filter is applied after the all-names pre-scan, so a narrowed run still validates `[workload].requires`/`.after` against the full fleet.
2. **User Setup** (`libexec/workload-ensure-user`): Runs as `ExecStartPre` in each workload service. Configures subordinate UID/GID ranges, creates home and volume directories, writes the EnvironmentFile, and enables linger.
3. **Workload Services**: Per-workload systemd services that run `podman run` as dedicated `_wl-<name>` users with rootless podman. Default service type is `Type=exec` (activates when podman execs the container process). `Type=notify` is available via `[resources] service_type = "notify"` but is **structurally incompatible** with this architecture, so `Type=exec` stays the default — this is settled, not a pending question. The root cause: systemd attributes an incoming `sd_notify` datagram to the unit owning the *sender's* cgroup, and under rootless + linger the process that emits `READY=1` always lives in `user@<uid>.service`'s cgroup, never in `workload-<name>.service`'s. So the notification is credited to the user manager (the wrong unit) and `workload-<name>.service` never sees it; no `NotifyAccess` tweak on the workload unit can fix this, because the sender is not in that unit's cgroup at all. Both sdnotify policies fail identically for this reason (verified on Fedora 44 / systemd 259, 2026-06-21): with `--sdnotify=conmon` the sender is conmon; with `--sdnotify=healthy` (which additionally requires a healthcheck) podman *does* send `READY=1` once the container is healthy, but the emitter is the re-exec'd libpod podman (`waitForHealthy`), which has migrated into `…/user@<uid>.service/…/podman-<pid>.scope` — same cgroup as conmon, same misattribution (systemd logs `user@<uid>.service: Got notification message from PID …, but reception only permitted for main PID …`). The earlier `--cgroups=split` explanation named the symptom; ADR 001 option 1b does not change the outcome because the notifier is user-manager-resident either way. Use podman-native `--health-cmd` + `workloadctl health`/`update`'s health-verified flow for readiness instead (those work under 1b). The VM substrate's `Type=notify` is unaffected — `workload-vm-notify` sends `READY=1` from a process inside the system unit's own cgroup. Cgroup placement uses **ADR 001 option 1b**: the generator emits a `user@<uid>.service.d/50-workload.conf` drop-in that redirects each workload's user manager into `workloads.slice` (`Slice=workloads.slice`). The container payload follows the user manager and lands at `workloads.slice/user@<uid>.service/…/libpod-<id>.scope` — inside the aggregate slice. Per-workload resource caps (`MemoryHigh`, `CPUWeight`, etc.) go on the same drop-in as `[Service]` directives; per-container caps (`--memory`, `--cpus`, `--pids-limit`, `--device-read-bps/write-bps`) are passed as podman flags and bind natively via the user manager's delegated subtree. There is no `cgroup_exec.py` placement shim — plain `sudo -u` exec works because the container is user-manager-resident. Podman's native `--health-cmd` healthcheck timer fires in the user manager and `--health-on-failure` works without any system-manager replacement. `ExecStopPost=-podman rm -f -t0` is emitted on each container unit because `KillMode=control-group` can't reach the payload (it lives in the user manager's cgroup subtree, not the system unit's). See `docs/adr/001-container-cgroup-placement.md`. Each workload's *head* unit runs two cleanup `ExecStartPre` steps before any other podman call: `ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/podman system migrate` then `ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/rm -f /run/user/<uid>/libpod/tmp/pause.pid /run/user/<uid>/libpod/tmp/ns_handles`. The problem: a libpod pause process left over from a previous service invocation gets migrated into `podman-pause-*.scope` under `user@<uid>.service` by any host-side podman call and survives restarts, but its mount namespace pins the old invocation's already-deleted `PrivateTmp` `/tmp`; the next `podman run` takes the rootless join shortcut (`can_use_shortcut` → `join_namespace_or_die`, which ignores `--userns` — so this is independent of keep-id vs host userns) into that stale pause, and pasta then fails its sandbox mount of `/tmp` with ENOENT and the unit restart-loops. `migrate` alone does not fully close this (`runtime_migrate.go` returns before `stopPauseProcess()` if any container stop errors), so the tolerant `rm` of `pause.pid`+`ns_handles` is the belt-and-suspenders: it makes the join shortcut fall through so podman builds a *fresh* pause in the live mount ns. Host-verified 2026-06-28 (both `--userns=keep-id` and `--userns=host` fail identically against an armed stale pause; the `rm` makes both start clean). Member services must *not* run either step (they would kill the pause out from under live pod infra / sibling containers).
4. **CLI** (`bin/workloadctl` + `lib/cmd_*.py` + `lib/substrate.py`): Docker/kubectl-like argparse CLI for creating, enabling, disabling, updating, and inspecting workloads. `bin/workloadctl` is a thin (~330-line) argument-parser/dispatcher; each verb's body lives in its own `lib/cmd_<verb>.py` module — `cmd_enable`, `cmd_disable`, `cmd_cleanup`, `cmd_create`, `cmd_validate`, `cmd_diagnose`, `cmd_edit`, `cmd_info`, `cmd_images`, `cmd_stats`, `cmd_health`, `cmd_doctor`, `cmd_drift`, `cmd_secret`, `cmd_catalog`, `cmd_backup`, `cmd_update`, plus the few that keep a small family together (`cmd_lifecycle` = start/stop/restart/recreate/reboot/build, `cmd_inspect` = list/status, `cmd_interact` = logs/exec/shell/cp/incant). The provisioning machinery those verbs share (preflight, user creation, image transfer, unit generation, host-setup hooks, SELinux policy) lives in `lib/provisioning.py`, deliberately outside the `cmd_*` namespace: it is library code with several command-layer callers, and `tests/test_layering.py` binds the "raise, never exit" rule to exactly the non-`cmd_*` modules. Substrate-variant verbs (status, health, stats, logs, exec/shell, start/stop/restart/reboot, update/recreate, rollback, backup, incant) route through the **Substrate port** (`lib/substrate.py`); container interactions use `lib/podman.py` (typed Podman wrapper returning structured data from `podman inspect --format=json` rather than go-template strings).

   **Exit-code boundary (enforced): the library core raises, only the CLI leaf exits.** `sys.exit()` is allowed in `bin/workloadctl` and `lib/cmd_*.py`, and nowhere else in `lib/`. Everything else — `workload_lib`, `workloadctl_core`, `substrate`, `substrate_container`, `substrate_vm`, `backup`, `podman`, `qmp`, `unit_file`, `validation`, `vm`, `secrets_template`, `service_runtime`, `imagebuild` — raises a typed exception, and `_run_cli()` in `bin/workloadctl` maps it to a code: `UsageError` → 2, `LifecycleError` → the returncode of the systemctl/podman call that failed, `NotRoot`/`ProvisionFailed`/`WorkloadMasked`/`WorkloadUserNotFound`/`FileNotFoundError` → 1, anything else → traceback + "this looks like a workloadctl bug". `ProvisionFailed`, `BackupError` and `NotApplicable` are also caught at call sites that must keep going (`update --all` tallies per-workload failures rather than dying on the first). The reason is that `SystemExit` inherits `BaseException` so it passes straight through `except Exception:` — harmless at a leaf, a trapdoor in a helper, which takes the process down past a caller that meant to recover. `tests/test_layering.py` walks the AST of every non-`cmd_` module in `lib/` and fails the suite if a `sys.exit`/`os._exit` call appears, so this is a checked invariant, not a convention.

   **`--dry-run` exists only where a truthful plan can be computed** — `disable` (`_disable_plan`) and `update` (`_update_plan`), plus `cleanup`, which defaults to it. Both plans are built read-only *before* any mutation and returned as lines, rather than by walking the real teardown with the writes switched off: a plan that shares the mutating path is only as trustworthy as the last guard someone remembered to add. They enumerate from the same sources the real path acts on (`workload_run_files`, the passwd db, `/etc/subuid`, the data dir) and report only what is actually present, so what a plan doesn't list, the command won't touch. The other mutating verbs deliberately have no `--dry-run`: for most of them "would restart the service" is a restatement of the verb, not a plan, and a dry-run that cannot be wrong teaches operators to trust it. Applying a config edit is `recreate`, and previewing that edit is `drift` (which already generates into a temp dir and diffs) — not a third flag.

### Boot Flow

```
systemd-generators → workload-generator (shell) emits workload-generate.service
workload-generate.service → runs Python workload-generate script, which writes
                            sysusers configs + per-workload unit files into
                            /run/systemd/system/ (After=sysinit Before=basic.target)
workload-{name}-setup.service → systemd-sysusers creates user; workload-ensure-user
                                configures subuid/subgid, home dir, EnvironmentFile, linger
workload-{name}.service → individual containers start via podman run
```

**Every emitted file is stamped with the build that wrote it** —
`# Generated by workload-generate (<version-release>)`, from `WORKLOADCTL_VERSION`
(`workload_lib`), which the RPM's `%install` injects as `_version.py` and which
`--version` also reports. Units live in `/run` and are rewritten only at boot or
by `enable`, so `dnf upgrade workloadctl` on a package host leaves running
workloads on the *previous* generator's output with nothing else to say so:
neither the TOML's nor the unit's mtime moved, which is exactly what
`units_outdated()` compares. `units_from_other_build()` reads the stamp back and
`doctor`/`diagnose`/`status` report the skew; the remedy is `workloadctl enable
<name>` (or a reboot). `drift` deliberately **normalizes the stamp away** before
comparing — it answers "do the running units match what this TOML would
produce", and letting a build bump mark every workload as drifted is how a
signal stops being read. On a bootc host the skew cannot arise: new code is live
only after a reboot, and that boot regenerates.

### User Management

- Username: `_wl-{name}` (e.g., `_wl-webserver`)
- UID range: 10000-52948 (42,949 max workloads)
- Subuid formula: `600100000 + (uid_offset * 65536)`, count=65536, where
  `uid_offset = uid - UID_MIN`. The base clears Fedora `useradd`'s own subid
  window (`SUB_UID_MIN=524288`), which a lower base overlaps at low UIDs.
  Authoritative in `workload_lib.derived_subid_range()`; the ranges are written
  by `workload_lib.append_subid_entries()`. `workload-ensure-user` grandfathers
  an existing entry rather than correcting it (shifting a mapping under a
  running container corrupts its namespace), so drift off the formula is
  permanent and silent — `diagnose`/`doctor`'s `subid_derived` and
  `subid_overlap` checks are the only thing that reports it
- Home directory: `/var/lib/workloads/{name}`
- Shell: `/usr/sbin/nologin`

### Network Modes

- `pasta` (default): Isolated networking with port forwarding (Podman 5.3+)
- `host`: Share host network namespace
- `none`: No networking
- Custom named networks for container-to-container communication

### Logging

Container stdout/stderr go to the host journal via `--log-driver=passthrough`
(podman hands the unit's journal stream fds to the container), with
`SyslogIdentifier=` set to the container name so lines read
`workload-<name>[pid]: ...` (`workload-<wl>-<ctr>` for pod/bridge members).
Passthrough stores each line exactly once — the journald driver kept a second,
untagged copy via the unit's stdout relay. Filter container output with
`journalctl -t workload-<name>`; `workloadctl logs` wraps journalctl, OR-ing the
unit with `SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER=` so passthrough app output is included (a unit-only
filter misses it — journald attributes it to the user manager's cgroup).
`podman logs` does not work with passthrough (podman keeps no copy).

### CLI output: prose vs. output

`lib/cli_log.py` owns the CLI's **prose** — what a command says *about* what it
is doing (progress, status, diagnostics). `info()` goes to stdout,
`warn()`/`error()` to stderr, so severity survives a redirect. Everything a
command was *asked* to produce — reports, `--dry-run` plans, JSON documents,
`incant`/`logs`/`stats` passthrough — stays on plain `print()`.

That split is the whole reason `--quiet` is safe: it raises the level to
WARNING, so it can silence narration but never a failure, and never the answer.
`--json` suppresses prose the same way *and* reserves stdout for the result
object the mutating verbs emit via `emit_result()` (shape in `docs/cli.md`), so
`update --all --json | jq` can't choke on a progress line. `bin/workloadctl`
calls `cli_log.configure()` once from the parsed args, and the exit-code ladder
in `_run_cli()` calls `emit_failure()` so a command that dies still leaves a
result document behind. Handlers resolve `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` per record
rather than binding at import, so a redirected caller (the test suite) still
captures what we write.

`--quiet`/`--json` are offered only on the verbs that mutate a workload (enable,
disable, start, stop, restart, reboot, recreate, build, update, rollback) — the
ones whose narration goes through cli_log. Offering the flag where it wasn't
honored would be a lie.

### Operations log

`lib/oplog.py` appends one JSON object per mutated workload to
`/var/lib/workloads/<name>/operations.log` — the `--json` result row plus `ts`,
`command`, `ok`, `user` and `user_source`. It hangs off `cli_log.emit_result()`,
the one call each verb already makes, so the log and `--json` are the same dict
and can't drift; a verb that learns to report something new records it with no
second call site. The administrative verbs (`create`/`init`/`duplicate`/
`install`/`edit`/`backup`/`restore`/`cp`) call `emit_result()` too even though
they own no `--json` document: with `json_mode` off it feeds the log and nothing
else. `secret` (host-global credstore) and `cleanup` (reaps orphans that have no
workload left to own a record) stay out.

`oplog.RECORDED_RESULTS` / `IGNORED_RESULTS` classify every `result` string a verb
can emit — **a new verb must add its result string to one of them.** It's an
allowlist because `update --all` reports `"unchanged"` for a fleet that didn't
move, and a denylist that hadn't heard of that string appended a no-op line per
workload on every scheduled run, forever (nothing rotates this file). An
unclassified string is recorded *and* warned about: losing an operation is worse
than keeping a doubtful one, and the warning is what sends you here.

The config-authoring verbs run before `enable` ever creates `/var/lib/workloads/
<name>/`, so `record()` makes that root on demand for any workload that has a
config. A name with no config gets a warning and no directory — otherwise a typo
would leave something `cleanup` reads as an orphan.

It is a **record, not an audit trail** — only root can run these verbs and root
can equally delete the file, so it is worthless as a tamper-evident control and
isn't offered as one. Its value is the half `sudo`'s own journal entry misses:
not *that* someone ran `update web`, but that the update moved nginx from
1f2e3d4c to 9a8b7c6d and rolled back on a failed health check.

`user` comes from the kernel's audit **loginuid** first (`/proc/self/loginuid`),
falling back to `SUDO_USER` and then the real uid — recorded as `user_source`
`login` / `sudo` / `system`. loginuid is the only unforgeable source and the only
one that survives `su -`; and its absence positively identifies automation, so a
timer-driven `update --all` reads as `system` rather than as an indistinguishable
bare `root`.

Placement is load-bearing: at the workload *root*, beside `state/` and `data/`
rather than inside either — so backup (which captures only `data/`) doesn't
import one host's history into a restored workload, and the rootless
`_wl-<name>` user (who owns `state/`) can't touch its own record. `--purge`
rmtree's the root and takes the log with it, which is coherent: the workload is
gone. Dry-runs and reports record nothing. Writes are best-effort — a missing
directory warns once on stderr and the command carries on. No rotation (a few KB
a year).

The workload root's other bookkeeping file, `provenance.json`, sits there for the
same reasons and answers a different question: **which ostree deployment this
`/var` state belongs to.** `/etc` is per-deployment and `/var` is shared, so
every piece of workload *identity* (the TOML, the `_wl-*` passwd line, the
`subuid` range) is per-deployment while its *state* is not — and `bootc rollback`,
which deletes nothing, therefore manufactures orphans: state whose workload has
no config here, which is precisely `cleanup`'s definition. `workload-ensure-user`
stamps the root with the booted deployment's `<csum>.<serial>` on every run (last
*provisioned* under, not created under — create-only stamping would make cleanup
skip the ordinary "operator deleted a TOML" sweep), and `cleanup` spares state
whose stamp names a deployment that still exists but isn't booted, reporting it
under "State from another deployment — not swept". Every uncertainty — no
`/ostree`, no stamp, a corrupt stamp, a pruned deployment — falls back to the
pre-stamp behavior, because nothing in this mechanism may ever *cause* a
deletion. The deployment id comes from resolving the cmdline's `ostree=` symlink
(its own csum is the **boot** checksum, not the deployment's) and existence is a
`glob('/ostree/deploy/*/deploy/<id>')` — the stateroot is a variable, and `/var`
may be a separate filesystem shared by all of them. `lib/deployment.py` carries
the full table. The UID and subid range are deliberately **not** stamped: the
owning UID of `<root>/data` is one `stat` away, and a copy could only go stale
and compete with `/etc/subuid`.

### Multi-Container Workloads

A workload may run more than one container under the same `_wl-<name>` user, sharing home directory and lifecycle. `workload.mode` selects the topology:

- `single` (default for `[container]`): one container, one service file at `workload-<name>.service`.
- `pod` (default for `[[containers]]`): all containers share one network namespace via `podman pod create`; sibling containers talk on `localhost`; ports are published once at the workload level.
- `bridge`: each container has its own netns on an auto-created `workload-<name>-net` bridge network; containers resolve each other by container short-name via the bridge's built-in DNS; ports are published per container.

Generated unit layout for multi-container workloads:

```
workload-<name>.service              # oneshot umbrella, pulls in everything
workload-<name>-setup.service        # sysusers + workload-ensure-user
workload-<name>-pod.service          # pod mode only — podman pod create
workload-<name>-net.service          # bridge mode only — podman network create
workload-<name>-<container>.service  # one per [[containers]] entry
```

Stopping the umbrella tears everything down (`PartOf=`). The CLI accepts `<workload>/<container>` for container-targeted commands (`exec`, `shell`, `logs`, `health`); lifecycle and most introspection commands take a bare `<workload>`. The generator normalizes single- and multi-container shapes through `normalize_containers()` so single-container TOMLs produce byte-identical units to before. See `docs/workloads.md` and `docs/schema-reference.toml` for the full schema; `workloads/webproxy-demo/workload.toml` is the smallest working bridge-mode example.

### Substrate dispatch

The substrate (container vs VM) is a first-class dimension, orthogonal to the verb. `lib/substrate.py` defines a `Substrate` abstract port with a small set of **primitives** — `liveness`, `resource_usage`, `logs`, `exec`/`open_shell`, `lifecycle(action)`, `reprovision`, `rollback_targets`/`rollback_to`, `capture(consistency)`, `endpoints`, `addresses`, `teardown`/`teardown_plan`, `control`, `gating_units` — plus the exception vocabulary (`NotApplicable`, `ProvisionFailed`, `BackupError`, `LifecycleError`) and the `get_substrate(config, manager)` router. The two implementations live beside it, one module each: `lib/substrate_container.py` (`ContainerSubstrate`) and `lib/substrate_vm.py` (`VMSubstrate`). Both import the port for the ABC and the exceptions, so `get_substrate()` imports them inside its body rather than at module scope — the router is the only place that has to know both, and only at call time. `get_substrate()` resolves the implementation from the **declaration** (presence of `[vm]`, i.e. `config.is_vm`), never from runtime state. Each substrate-variant verb is written once and composes primitives; the substrate-specific delta lives only in the port.

The one primitive with a shared body is `capture`: `lib/backup.py` stages the TOML, the credential blobs and the precious `data/` tree into a temp dir and tars it, and the substrates differ only in how they quiesce the workload first (systemd stop vs QMP vCPU pause), so that difference stays in the callers.

Required primitives are `@abstractmethod`s, so a substrate cannot exist without them. Optional ones (`resource_usage`, `logs`, `endpoints`, `addresses`, `reprovision`, `teardown`, `teardown_plan`) have a base-class default — `NotApplicable` with a self-documenting reason for most, `[]` for the teardown pair, since a substrate with no state of its own to remove is coherent rather than incapable — and a substrate opts in by overriding. The `(verb, substrate)` capability matrix is therefore **declared by what each class defines**, not maintained as a list: a verb a substrate can't serve reports "not applicable" rather than running a nonsensical command against it. `ContainerSubstrate` overrides `resource_usage`/`endpoints`/`reprovision` plus the teardown pair (subuid/subgid ranges, the `user@<uid>.service.d` drop-in); `VMSubstrate` overrides `resource_usage` (sourced from QMP, see below), `reprovision`, `addresses` (the guest's IP on the VM bridge) and the teardown pair (socket dir, and the shared bridge when the last bridged VM goes), and leaves `logs`/`endpoints` at the default. Two questions travel on two channels: a *capability* answer is `NotApplicable`, while "supported, nothing right now" is the type's empty value in band — `endpoints` returns `[]` with no ports published, `addresses` returns `[]` before the guest has a lease, `reprovision` returns `None` when already up to date. A new primitive should prefer an empty container to a `None` sentinel, so the nothing case has the same shape as the something case.

`resource_usage(json_out=True)` returns normalized rows keyed by `STAT_ROW_KEYS`, uniform across substrates so `stats --json` has one schema. A substrate with no source for a key reports `None`, not `0` — a VM has no block-I/O figure because nothing asks QEMU for `query-blockstats`, and a zero there would read as an idle disk rather than as a gap. The VM row is read from `qmp-metrics.sock` (the dedicated read-only monitor the Prometheus exporter also scrapes) via `lib/vm_metrics.py`, never from the control socket `qmp.sock`: a QMP monitor serves one client at a time, so a competing reader there could block `ExecStop`'s `system_powerdown` and force an unclean SIGKILL.

`gating_units()` is a diagnostics primitive: it names the systemd units that must succeed *before* the main service starts. Containers return `[]` (setup is an `ExecStartPre` on the main unit, so a failure surfaces there directly); a VM returns its `workload-<name>-setup.service` + `workload-<name>-build.service`, which run as separate `RemainAfterExit=yes` units. `status`/`_effective_state` walk these so a failed setup/build is reported as `failed` and the culprit unit is named, instead of the main service showing a bland `inactive`/`dependency failed` with the real cause buried.

### VM workloads

A TOML with a top-level `[vm]` section (mutually exclusive with `[container]`/`[[containers]]`) runs as a raw QEMU/KVM virtual machine under a systemd unit, via `VMSubstrate` and the `libexec/workload-vm-*` helpers (`workload-vm-build-disk`, `workload-vm-qmp`, `workload-vm-shutdown`, `workload-vm-notify`, `workload-vm-netdev`):

- **Disks** — a writable `system.qcow2` built once from the image source (rebuildable, with generational `system.qcow2.gen-N` rollback, `rollback_keep + 1` retained) plus an optional durable `data.qcow2`. `update`/`reprovision` rebuilds `system.qcow2`; `rollback` restores the previous generation.
- **Networking** — **passt** (ADR 006), not a bridge: it terminates the guest's stack in userspace and re-originates traffic as host sockets owned by `_wl-<name>`, so **the workload uid is the network identity** (unforgeable, unique, matchable as `meta skuid`). The guest is assigned the *host's* address, so it has no LAN identity; `exec`/`shell` reach it on a uid-derived management address (`127.128.0.0 + uid offset`, port 2222). `[vm.network].bridge` is the escape hatch for a VM that needs a real LAN identity — supported, and **unfiltered by design**. Egress policy is one nftables table (`inet workload_filter`, skeleton at `%{_datadir}/workloadctl/workload-filter.nft`) whose *elements* the units manage — never its rules; the file is applied on every VM start and is idempotent because it flushes the chain before re-adding rules, while set elements survive on the table. `egress` defaults to `"filtered"`, but the implicit allow that makes an empty allowlist workable is the per-workload proxy (step 4), so **until that lands `filtered` with an empty `allow` is a validation error** — every VM config must state a posture. `allow` is addresses and ports only, never hostnames (set elements are keyed on `ip`/`ip6 daddr`; a name would be resolved once at start and then be silently wrong). Break-glass: `nft delete table inet workload_filter`.
- **Boot/seed** — UEFI/OVMF firmware; cloud-init seed ISO from `[vm.cloud_init]` (user-data template + `template_vars`); a per-instance SSH key for CLI access. CLI verbs reach a VM over SSH (`exec`/`shell`) or QMP (`incant`, lifecycle, `capture`), not podman.

`workloads/virtual-forgejo/workload.toml` is the live example; `docs/schema-reference.toml` documents `[vm]`, `[vm.cloud_init]`, and `[vm.network]`.

### Lifecycle: pet vs cattle

`[workload] lifecycle` (default `"cattle"`) declares lifecycle intent, honored per-substrate. **Cattle** containers are ephemeral — the generator appends `--rm`, so the writable overlay is destroyed on every stop/start (including a plain reboot) and rebuilt from the image. **Pet** containers reuse the overlay (`podman create` once + `start`/`stop`, no `--rm`; the graphroot lives under `/var` and survives reboots and bootc updates) and snapshot the overlay to a timestamped local image before any destructive verb (`recreate`/`update`). A **pet VM** skips `system.qcow2` rotation on `reprovision`/`update`, keeping the durable disk. Pet reclassifies a workload's `home/`/system disk from rebuildable-and-backup-skipped to precious-and-backup-included.

### Secrets

Uses systemd credentials (`systemd-creds`) for secret management:
- Encryption at rest via AES256-GCM with TPM2 or host keys
- Runtime decryption into RAM-only tmpfs
- Per-workload isolation
- `${SECRET:name}` syntax in environment variables for auto-detection
- Portable export/import between machines

### SELinux confinement

A workload that needs rights beyond the stock container domain sets
`[security].selinux_policy = true` and ships a policy file. Each such workload
gets its **own** SELinux type (`wl_<name>.process`) rather than adding rules to
the shared `container_t`. This matters because a `semodule` load is global: a
rule written against `container_t` widens *every* container on the host, so the
desktop/telemetry workloads' device and journal grants would otherwise leak
host-wide. Per-workload types keep each workload's extra rights scoped to
itself, and — because the type is keyed on the workload name — a duplicated
workload gets an independently loadable/removable module.

The policy is written in **CIL** (Common Intermediate Language, the IR the
SELinux userspace compiles `.te`/`.pp` down to), not `.te`, for two reasons:

- **Inheritance.** `(block wl_<name> (blockinherit container) ...)` stamps out a
  full copy of the base `container` domain and adds the workload's extra rules
  on top. A flat `.te` rule on `container_t` can't be "copied per workload";
  a bare `typeattribute container_domain` is not a complete container domain
  (the container won't even start). Inheriting udica's base block is what
  supplies the full domain.
- **Namespacing + direct load.** CIL blocks namespace their types
  (`wl_<name>.process`), so two workloads never collide on a shared type, and
  `semodule -i` loads `.cil` directly — no `checkmodule`/`semodule_package`
  compile step (and no `checkpolicy` dependency).

Authoring is done with **udica** against a running container; it emits the CIL
block and the base templates (`/usr/share/udica/templates/*.cil`) that
workloadctl loads alongside the workload module on `enable`. The enable-time
loader lives in `lib/provisioning.py` (`apply_selinux_policy`); the
`[security].selinux_policy` flag is documented in `docs/schema-reference.toml`.

**All of the above is the container path. VM workloads confine differently**
(ADR 006 step 3), and the difference is easy to get wrong:

- **QEMU runs as `svirt_t`, unconditionally and without the flag.** Not a
  per-workload type: `svirt_t` is the distro's own domain for a hypervisor
  process hosting an untrusted guest, and re-deriving it would be the mistake
  the per-workload argument above is *not* making — there is fifteen years of
  encoded knowledge to inherit, where a container workload has none. The
  transition is a `runcon` prefix in `libexec/workload-vm-notify`, because
  systemd execs from `init_t` and the policy has no `init_t → svirt_t`
  transition; `unconfined_service_t → virt_domain` is what makes it work.
- **MCS categories are deliberately unused.** libvirt needs them because all its
  VMs share one uid; ours each run as their own `_wl-<name>`, so DAC already
  separates them.
- **So `[security].selinux_policy` means something different on a VM.** The
  `wl_<name>.process` type it declares has exactly one consumer — the generator
  passing it to podman — and a VM makes no podman call. A VM's `policy.cil` is a
  *delta against `svirt_t`*.
- **Two host-global pieces ship outside that flag:** the `svirt_image_t`
  fcontext rule per VM workload (semanage at enable, gated on `is_vm`, because
  labelling is a precondition for booting rather than optional hardening), and
  `security/workload-vm.cil` — a virtiofsd domain plus the two grants QEMU's
  native passt netdev needs — which the RPM loads once.

Three traps worth carrying forward if you touch this. A `filecon` in a bundle's
`policy.cil` under a path workloadctl registers with `semanage` is **silently
ignored**, because `file_contexts.local` outranks the base `file_contexts`
wholesale (`validate` warns). The shipped policy **dontaudits** the rule passt
needs under a QEMU-native netdev, so an ordinary AVC harvest will not show it —
run `semodule -DB` before concluding a harvest is complete. And **no unit that
transitions into one of our domains may set `NoNewPrivileges=`** (nor
`DynamicUser=`, which implies it): NNP makes the kernel refuse any transition
not *bounded* by the calling domain, and none of ours are bounded by `init_t`.
The symptom is a bare `203/EXEC` "Permission denied" on a mode-0755 binary, with
`op=security_bounded_transition` in the audit log and nothing else pointing at
the cause. The seccomp-implying options (`PrivateDevices=`, `ProtectKernel*=`,
`SystemCallFilter=`, ...) are fine despite the documentation's phrasing —
systemd only forces NNP for those when the *manager* lacks `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`,
which never holds for a system service.

A harvest is only ever as good as the workout behind it, and this is where the
virtiofsd domain has been wrong twice: the module is a list of the classes
someone happened to exercise, so a share can pass every test and still deny
`ln -s`. `security/workload-vm.cil` records the workout its current list came
from — extend that before extending the rules.

### Hostname policy: the per-workload proxy (step 4)

`[vm.network].hosts` gives one VM its own tinyproxy, confined by
`security/workload-proxy.cil` (14 rules, host-global, RPM-loaded like the
virtiofsd domain). Three non-obvious things hold it together:

- **The proxy runs as the workload's own user, so `meta skuid` cannot tell it
  from the guest** — and under default-deny that means the drop catches the
  proxy too, leaving hostname policy permitting nothing. The discriminator is
  the **control group** (`wl_proxy_cg` in the filter skeleton), which systemd
  assigns and a guest can neither enter nor forge. Widening by port instead is
  the bypass the default-deny chain exists to close. The proxy unit's `Slice=`
  is pinned for this reason: the match is `level 2`, so the cgroup path must
  stay two components deep.
- **The guest reaches one advertised address** (`192.0.2.1:3128`) and a uid-keyed
  nat map sends it to its own instance. The proxy's client ACL must `Allow` that
  address, not just loopback — the source the host picks for a route to itself
  *is* that address, and getting this wrong 403s every request while nothing
  looks broken.
- **A permissive AVC harvest is nearly useless here.** tinyproxy exits 70 on the
  first denial, so the harvest stops at the first gate; the module was finished
  by iterating under *enforcing*, one gate per round. The opposite of how
  `wlvfsd_t` was derived.

### The credential broker

`[vm.network].broker = true` entitles one VM to reach `libexec/agent-broker`, a
standalone program this package ships and does not enable. The guest never holds
a provider API key: it dials the same advertised literal every guest gets
(`192.0.2.1:8081`), a uid-keyed nat map sends it to the broker, and the broker
attaches the real credential on the way out. Guest→broker is plain HTTP, so no
CA goes into the guest and nothing breaks certificate pinning.

- **Identity is the uid owning the far end of the connection**, read out of
  `/proc/net/tcp`. The host assigns it and a guest cannot forge it, which is why
  two guests dialling one literal can hold different keys. It fails *silently*
  when it fails: from a user namespace that cannot map a workload's uid, every
  caller reads as the overflow uid and they all merge into one identity. The
  unit therefore must not set `PrivateUsers=`, and the program refuses to start
  when it can prove that is happening.
- **The upstream is fixed by config and never taken from a request.** That is
  the whole security property — a broker that forwarded to a guest-chosen
  destination would be an SSRF pivot with a credential welded to it.
- **`libexec/workload-vm-broker` is a different thing**: the per-VM map element,
  run from the VM unit, which deliberately does not start, stop or check the
  broker. Its address must match the broker's listen defaults, asserted by
  `tests/test_vm_broker.py` — a drift there is indistinguishable from the broker
  being down. It runs for *every* non-bridged VM, installing the element or
  removing one, because uids are reused and an entitlement must not outlive the
  workload it was granted to.
- **Admission is bounded per caller, not just in total.** 32 connections
  overall, 8 for any one caller, and 60 seconds of no progress ends a
  connection. A single global bound is a denial-of-service lever rather than a
  protection: one sandbox opening 32 sockets and sending nothing denied the
  broker to every other sandbox, which is measured in
  `tests/test_broker_request.py`.
- **Never proven end to end.** Both halves have unit tests; no real guest has
  ever dialled a real broker. `tests/manual/broker_rig.py` is the rig for it.

### Packet capture (step 5)

`workloadctl pcap` writes a non-terminating `log` rule into the
security-critical `inet workload_filter` table and reads it back through
`tcpdump -i nflog:<uid - UID_MIN>`. Things that bite here:

- **Capture gets its own chains — `pcap_output` (at `filter - 10`) and
  `pcap_input` — and never writes into the skeleton's `output` chain.** Two
  reasons, and both were silent failures before: `nft add rule` appends, so a
  log rule in `output` lands *below* the terminating drop and never matches for
  a filtered workload; and the skeleton carries `flush chain ... output`, so
  every VM start deleted any running capture's rule. Being ahead of policy also
  means dropped packets are captured, which is usually the point.
- **Deleting a capture chain is guarded on it being empty.** `nft delete chain`
  does *not* refuse a non-empty base chain — it succeeds and takes the rules
  with it, so an unguarded delete ended every concurrent capture.
- **The skeleton's `ct mark set` is guarded on the uid RANGE, not
  `@wl_filtered`.** The mark is attribution, not policy; `-Q in` selects on it,
  so guarding it on the policy set made inbound capture silently empty for
  containers and `egress = "open"` VMs.
- **nft deletes rules by handle, never by text.** A text-shaped delete fails
  silently under a tolerant runner, leaving a log rule nobody owns. Teardown
  reads live handles and narrows them to the workload's nflog group so a
  concurrent capture keeps its own rule.
- **SIGTERM skips `finally`.** Python's default disposition terminates without
  unwinding, so `systemctl stop` — the normal path — was the one that never
  finalized a guest-side file. `libexec/workload-pcap` turns SIGTERM into
  `SystemExit`; the unit's `ExecStopPost` covers `kill -9`.
- **A confined QEMU cannot write an operator's `-w` path**, and fails on DAC
  before SELinux is consulted — silently, with `object-add` accepted and no
  file created. Guest-side captures are staged in `/run/workload-vm/<name>/`
  (labelled `qemu_var_run_t` by step 3) and moved on finalize.
- **Guest-side timestamps are wrong by VM uptime + the host's UTC offset.**
  Measured at −29,407 s on a PDT host. The offset is measured with a probe
  packet, never derived from guest uptime — deriving it leaves the timezone
  term in place, silently, on every non-UTC host.

The plan travels from CLI to helper as JSON so `--dry-run` and the run cannot
disagree. `diagnose` reports a live capture, so the extra rule is explained
rather than discovered.

## Key Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `workloadctl pcap <name> [FILTER]` | Capture traffic; `-D` lists vantages, `--dry-run` prints the exact nft rule first |
| `workloadctl catalog` | List shippable bundles under `/usr/share/workloadctl/workloads/` |
| `workloadctl init <bundle> [--as <name>]` | Stamp a catalog bundle into `/etc/workloads.d/<name>/workload.toml` (sets `bundle` when name diverges) |
| `workloadctl duplicate <src> <new>` | Copy a live workload (alias `clone`); resolves `bundle` to the source's, lints host-global settings |
| `workloadctl create` | Scaffold a from-scratch workload TOML from flags (`--image …`) |
| `workloadctl enable` | Create user, transfer image, start service |
| `workloadctl disable` | Stop service, optionally purge user/data (`--dry-run` prints the teardown plan) |
| `workloadctl start` | Start workload service |
| `workloadctl stop` | Stop workload service |
| `workloadctl restart` | Bounce the workload service (keeps the container overlay / VM disks + seed; does **not** apply TOML edits — that's `recreate`) |
| `workloadctl reboot` | Restart the workload (container: keeps the overlay; VM: guest reboot) |
| `workloadctl update` | Pull new image / rebuild VM disk and recreate (automatic rollback on failure; `--dry-run` prints what it would pull and restart) |
| `workloadctl recreate` | Recreate from current config (destroys a cattle overlay; rotates VM `system.qcow2`) |
| `workloadctl rollback` | Roll back to the previous image (VM: restore previous disk generation); `--list` shows targets |
| `workloadctl status` | Show workload status |
| `workloadctl logs` | View workload logs (container output / VM service journal) |
| `workloadctl list` | List all configured workloads |
| `workloadctl info` | Show detailed workload information (incl. ports/uid-map/ps facets) |
| `workloadctl shell` | Open interactive shell (container exec / VM SSH) |
| `workloadctl exec` | Execute command inside the workload (container exec / VM SSH) |
| `workloadctl incant` | Run a command against the runtime control plane as the owning identity (container: `podman …` as `_wl-<name>`; VM: QMP) |
| `workloadctl edit` | Edit config in $EDITOR with validation |
| `workloadctl validate` | Validate TOML config (static, declaration-level) |
| `workloadctl diagnose` | Diagnose workload runtime setup (user, subuid, linger, SELinux), emits fixes |
| `workloadctl drift` | Show drift between generated and deployed systemd unit files (exits 1 if out of sync) |
| `workloadctl stats` | Show live resource usage (containers via podman; VMs via QMP, no `--follow`) |
| `workloadctl health` | Check health status (scriptable exit code) |
| `workloadctl secret` | Manage TPM2-encrypted credentials |
| `workloadctl backup` | Backup config, overrides, and durable data; `--consistency {cold,crash}` for VMs |
| `workloadctl restore` | Restore workload from backup archive |
| `workloadctl cleanup` | Find/remove orphaned workload users |

Most mutating commands require `sudo`. Read-only commands work as any user.

## Configuration (TOML)

Workloads are defined in `/etc/workloads.d/<name>/workload.toml`. Key sections:

- `[workload]` — name, enabled flag, `mode` (single/pod/bridge), `lifecycle` (pet/cattle, default cattle)
- `[container]` — image, command, pull policy, systemd mode, user, environment, health checks
- `[container.health]` — health check cmd, interval, timeout, retries, on_failure action
- `[container.environment]` — env vars, supports `${SECRET:name}` syntax
- `[setup]` — required_files that must exist before enable
- `[secrets]` — file-mounted systemd credentials
- `[devices]` — generic device passthrough, GPU (amd/nvidia), input, audio, virtualization flags
- `[security]` — userns mode (keep-id, host), extra_groups, capabilities, seccomp profile, `selinux_policy`
- `[network]` — mode (pasta/host/none/custom), ports, DNS
- `[resources]` — cpu-quota, cpu-weight, memory-max, memory-high, io-weight, tasks-max, shm-size, service_type (default: `exec`)
- `[volumes]` — host:container path mappings

VM workloads use a separate, mutually-exclusive set of sections:

- `[vm]` — image source (`image` or `cloud_image_url` + `cloud_image_checksum`), memory, vcpus, rollback_keep, data-disk size
- `[vm.cloud_init]` — user-data template + `template_vars` for per-instance seeding
- `[vm.network]` — `ports` (published, container convention), `egress` (`"filtered"` default / `"open"`), `allow` (`"<addr>:<port>"`, addresses only), `outbound_if` (pin egress to one host interface), `resolver` (`"host"` / `"none"`), and `bridge` (absent = passt; present = attach directly and be unfiltered). Presence of `bridge` IS the topology selector — there is no `mode` key. `egress`/`allow` alongside `bridge` is an error, not a no-op: a bridged guest sends from its own LAN address, so no host socket carries the uid.

## File Structure

```
bin/workloadctl                    # CLI dispatcher (argparse → lib/cmd_*.py)
lib/cmd_*.py                       # One module per verb (enable, disable, info, health, …)
lib/provisioning.py                # The provisioning steps enable/disable/recreate share (preflight, user creation, image transfer, unit generation, host-setup hook, SELinux policy)
lib/cli_log.py                     # CLI prose channel (info/warn/error, --quiet) + the mutating verbs' --json result object
lib/oplog.py                       # Per-workload operations log (/var/lib/workloads/<name>/operations.log, JSON Lines)
lib/substrate.py                   # Substrate port (ABC + exceptions + get_substrate router, computed capability matrix)
lib/substrate_container.py         # ContainerSubstrate (rootless podman)
lib/substrate_vm.py                # VMSubstrate (QEMU/KVM, SSH + QMP)
lib/backup.py                      # capture() implementation shared by both substrates
generators/workload-generator      # Tiny shell systemd generator (emits workload-generate.service)
generators/workload-generate       # Python script run by workload-generate.service at early boot
libexec/workload-ensure-user       # Per-workload user setup (ExecStartPre)
libexec/workload-vm-*              # VM helpers (build-disk, qmp, shutdown, notify, netdev)
libexec/agent-broker               # The credential broker: a standalone program, not a helper (shipped disabled)
libexec/workload-metrics           # Prometheus metrics exporter
lib/workloadctl_core.py            # WorkloadConfig / WorkloadManager (TOML loading, paths, lifecycle field)
lib/workload_lib.py                # Shared library (config parsing, UID allocation, VM bridge constants)
lib/podman.py                      # Typed Podman wrapper (JSON output, PodmanError, root/user modes)
lib/vm_metrics.py                  # VM metric collectors (QMP balloon/vCPU, qemu cgroup) shared by the exporter and `stats`
workloads/<bundle>/                # Shipped bundles: workload.toml (template declaration)
                                   #   co-located with control files (Containerfile, build.sh,
                                   #   setup.sh, policy.cil, cloud-init user-data — any subset)
docs/workloads.md                  # Full configuration guide
docs/workload-run-files.md         # Authoritative per-workload run-file topology (what disable/drift/inspect enumerate)
docs/cli.md                        # Complete CLI reference
docs/secrets.md                    # Secrets management guide
docs/agent-broker.md               # Credential broker: threat model, identity, operation
docs/agent-broker.toml.example     # Annotated broker config (installed to /usr/share/doc/workloadctl/)
docs/schema-reference.toml         # Annotated TOML schema with all options
docs/testing.md                    # Test-value rubric: rung model, oracle/contract/snapshot, deletion heuristic
systemd/                           # systemd units (workloads.slice, metrics timer)
completions/                       # Bash completions
seccomp-workload-baseline.json     # Default seccomp profile
tests/                             # Test suite
```

## Included Container Images

Pre-built container definitions ship in their bundle dir (`workloads/<bundle>/`):

- `smb-server` — Samba file sharing (guest shares, host networking)
- `wireguard-vpn` — WireGuard VPN client
- `socks5-vpn` — SOCKS5 proxy over WireGuard
- `dns-vpn` — DNS resolver over WireGuard
- `pihole-vpn` — Pi-hole DNS + WireGuard VPN
- `proxy-stack` — Squid cache + Pi-hole + WireGuard (all-in-one)
- `squid` — Squid caching proxy
- `grafana` — Grafana dashboards for workload monitoring
- `desktop-vnc` — VNC-accessible Wayland desktop

## Deliberate non-adoptions

These patterns were considered and explicitly rejected:

- **Stdlib-only constraint.** `lib/` has no third-party dependencies; all imports are stdlib + `tomllib`. The rationale: the tool ships inside a bootc image RPM. Adding pip/venv machinery to a system Python package creates unresolvable version-conflict surface; keeping everything stdlib means `python3 -m unittest` "just works" and the RPM only needs `python3`.

- **`podman secret` for runtime secrets.** Rejected: podman secrets are stored as plaintext JSON on disk under the user's homedir (`$HOME/.local/share/containers/storage/secrets/`). workloadctl uses systemd credentials (`systemd-creds`, AES256-GCM, TPM2-bound) instead — encrypted blobs that only decrypt in-process to a tmpfs mount at runtime. See `docs/secrets.md`.

- **`podman auto-update` for image updates.** Rejected: auto-update is keyed on the container having an `io.containers.autoupdate` label and uses `sd_notify` to signal readiness. workloadctl's update flow does a health-verified rollback (pull → recreate → health check → rollback on failure), which auto-update can't replicate. The `workloadctl update` verb is the correct path.

- **Quadlet (systemd `.container` units).** Rejected in favour of the current generator approach; see `docs/adr/001-container-cgroup-placement.md` option 3. Quadlet generates units at daemon-reload time, not boot-generator time, which means the units don't exist when `workload-generate.service` runs (`Before=basic.target`). Cgroup placement under Quadlet also hardcodes the system unit cgroup tree, blocking the option-1b `workloads.slice` redirect. Keeping an explicit generator preserves full control of the unit content and ordering.

- **Rootful `--userns=auto` (per-container UID remapping).** Rejected; see `docs/adr/001-container-cgroup-placement.md` option 4. Rootful podman with `--userns=auto` remaps container UIDs to an unprivileged range but still runs the container manager as root — any container escape exposes the full root privilege of the host. workloadctl's dedicated `_wl-<name>` users run the podman *process* itself unprivileged. The blast radius of a container escape is bounded to the workload user, not root.

## Deliberate non-features

These capabilities are out of scope for a single-host homelab workload manager and there are no intentions to add them:

- **Multi-node scheduling and cluster orchestration.** Workloads bind to one host; there is no distributed scheduling, workload migration, or peer discovery.

- **Service mesh.** No sidecar injection, no transparent network policies, no distributed tracing substrate.

- **HA/failover.** No active-active clustering or automatic restart on a different node. If the host is down, workloads are down.

- **Secret rotation policy engine.** Secrets are operator-managed at deployment time; there is no automatic key rotation or credential freshening.

- **Cross-host orchestration.** Each host is managed independently. There is no global policy engine, topology discovery, or fleet-wide coordination.

## Trust model

While workloads run as individual user accounts, workload configs under `/etc/workloads.d/` are **root-equivalent, fully-trusted inputs**. The provisioning pipeline assumes configs are trusted:

- `[host].setup` hooks run arbitrary root scripts at enable time.
- `install`, `duplicate`, and `restore` write configs with root privilege.
- The generator and provisioning scripts execute all TOML directives without validation.

**Untrusted or third-party configs are out of scope for this tool.** A config with access to `/etc/workloads.d/` can request arbitrary capabilities, mount any path, and run setup commands as root. Never enable a workload from an untrusted TOML source.

### Image trust

Container images are governed by the host `/etc/containers/policy.json` (built from `policy-hypervisor.json.template` at the repo root), which is **refuse-by-default**: `"default": [{"type": "reject"}]` and no `""` scope under the docker transport. Eight scopes are listed. `registry.local` and `ghcr.io/<our-namespace>` require `sigstoreSigned` against `/etc/pki/containers/cosign.pub`; `docker.io`, bare `ghcr.io`, `quay.io`, `codeberg.org`, `mcr.microsoft.com` and `registry.fedoraproject.org` are `insecureAcceptAnything`. Anything outside those eight cannot be pulled at all. Most-specific-scope-wins is what lets a third-party `ghcr.io/<someone-else>` image through while our own `ghcr.io` namespace stays signature-enforced.

So: **our own images are signature-verified; third-party images are accepted unsigned, by design** — workloads must be able to consume public registries, and a homelab has no path to signatures upstream doesn't publish.

The compensating control is that **drift is confined to a deliberate verb**. `pull` is not an update-time setting: it becomes `podman run --pull=<policy>` in the unit's `ExecStart`, so `always`/`newer` re-pull on *every* service start — every boot, every restart — with no health check and no rollback. Shipped bundles therefore use `missing` or `never` only (enforced by `tests/test_workloads.py`); an image is pulled once and then held. Changing it means running `workloadctl update`, which pulls the current tag, tags the outgoing image as a rollback target, restarts, health-checks, and rolls back on failure (`lib/cmd_update.py`, `lib/substrate_container.py`).

Two consequences worth stating plainly. Nothing is digest-pinned, so `update` fetches whatever a tag now points at — "pinned" here means pinned *in time*, not pinned by content. And several third-party tags float without looking like it (`:vulkan`, `:server-vulkan`, `:default-cpu` move exactly like `:latest`); those bundles carry a comment saying so, because the tag alone misleads a reader in a way `:latest` does not.

`pull = "never"` means never *from a registry*, not never changes: `is_buildable` treats it as locally built, so root's image store still supplies it through the override channel (see `transfer_one_image`). A workload where every container is `never` is skipped by `update` entirely, with a build hint.
